tableS2.title: Table S2. Before, during and after the degree: how England, continental Europe, Hong Kong and the United States place breadth and professional formation around a three-year or four-year construction degree
rows: System
Before the degree
The degree
After the degree
What it shows for a 90-credit U.S. degree
England, Wales and Northern Ireland
compulsory schooling ends at 16; students then normally study three or four subjects, a range unusually narrow among the 24 countries compared (Hodgen et al., 2010)

360 credits in three years at 34 of 40 CIOB-accredited programs, 33 with a placement year offered; discipline 75% and general education 2% of the credits; 3,600 hours, 80 U.S. credits, of which 73 are discipline and projects

RICS: with an accredited degree and less than five years of experience, at least 24 months (400 days) of structured training before the final assessment (RICS, 2026a); CIOB chartership after at least three years of relevant experience with a built-environment honours degree, five otherwise (CIOB, n.d.)
a three-year degree works where breadth ends before it and professional formation continues after it
Continental Europe (Bologna)
not read in this study

180 ECTS in three years is the most widespread first-cycle workload (European Commission et al., 2024); RICS requires at least 360 UK credits or 180 ECTS for an accredited undergraduate award (RICS, 2026b)

81% of Bavarian university bachelor’s graduates go on to a master’s (Banschbach & Falk, 2017); of those who left Dutch higher education with a diploma in 2014/15, 37% held a university master’s and 11% a university bachelor’s (CBS, 2019)
the three-year degree is a first cycle, and most graduates continue
Hong Kong
six years of secondary school for all from the 2009/10 school year; under the old structure only about a third of students reached the last two school years (EMB, 2005)
four years since 2012, the added year meant to make room for general education (Jaffee, 2012); in the 8 programs with full module lists, discipline 45% and general education 27% of the credits
not read in this study
the fourth year was added to make room for general education
United States
nearly 2.5 million high school students took a dual enrollment course in 2022-23; Black students were 8% of dual enrollment and 13% of undergraduates (Fink, 2024)

120 credits or more in four years at every construction program with a published total, general education inside the degree: construction and business courses a mean 74.6 and mathematics and science 12.2 of 121.6 credits in the 81 modeled programs; 5,400 hours at 45 a credit; most earlier three-year paths squeezed a four-year program into three years, and take-up ranged from 2% to 19% of students (Weinstein, 2018)

CCM: 48 months of responsible-in-charge experience with a construction management degree accredited by ABET, ACCE or NAAB, 72 with any other four-year degree (CMCI, 2026); in a small survey, graduate admissions officers almost unanimously would not admit domestic applicants with fewer than 120 credits, though most were reconsidering (Marcus, 2026)
breadth and formation both sit inside the four years; a 90-credit degree has to move one of them out
notes: Composition of credits by content type from the module and course lists. U.S. credits by hours at 45 notional hours a semester credit and 10 a UK credit.

tableS7.title: Table S7. Potential stakeholder implications of reduced-credit construction management degrees, and the evidence behind each
rows: Stakeholder
Potential implications
Evidence and uncertainty
Students
Lower tuition requirements and potentially earlier workforce entry, balanced against changes in breadth, professional preparation and long-term earnings
Tuition and existing graduate earnings are observed or imputed (earnings imputed for 62 of 168 programs). Earlier completion and earnings outcomes of 90-credit graduates are not observed
Institutions
Reduced instructional commitments and potential recruitment opportunities, alongside changes in tuition revenue and enrollment
Financial outcomes depend on accounting assumptions, funding arrangements and actual enrollment responses
Employers
Potential access to graduates sooner, with concerns about technical preparation, communication and practical experience
Exploratory responses from 10 industry advisors at one accredited program, not representative evidence of employer preferences
Professional recognition
A shorter accredited degree may provide a route to professional practice, but its treatment by certification bodies and graduate institutions remains uncertain
Existing eligibility requirements are documented, but the recognition of future 90-credit degrees requires confirmation
notes: Denominators: the financial scenarios cover the 168 programs with a published total, tuition and earnings data, which include 80 of the 81 programs of the curriculum model; each scenario removes the published total less 90 credits, whatever pathway a program would take, and is not restricted to programs whose model design fits 90. The curriculum results are those of the 81 modeled programs.
